claim: Attention allows us to focus sensory processing on behaviorally relevant aspects of the visual world.
source: Attention allows us to focus sensory processing on behaviorally relevant aspects of the visual world.
evidence: This is a general statement about attention supported by established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: One potential mechanism of attention is a change in the gain of sensory responses.
source: One potential mechanism of attention is a change in the gain of sensory responses.
evidence: This statement reflects established theories in the attention literature.

claim: A Gaussian-shaped gain modulation results in changes to spatial tuning properties in a model of primate visual cortex.
source: Using a model of primate visual cortex we document how a Gaussian-shaped gain modulation results in changes to spatial tuning properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling experiments described in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 3.

claim: Forcing the model to use only changes in spatial tuning properties failed to produce any benefit in task performance.
source: Forcing the model to use only these changes failed to produce any benefit in task performance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results from the shift-only, receptive field structure, and shrinkage models shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: Gain alone was both necessary and sufficient to explain category detection and discrimination during attention.
source: Instead, we found that gain alone was both necessary and sufficient to explain category detection and discrimination during attention.
evidence: This is supported by the gain-only model results in Figure 7 and the necessity/sufficiency tests in Figure 8.

claim: Spatial attention allows observers to detect targets with higher accuracy.
source: Deploying goal-directed spatial attention towards visual locations allows observers to detect targets with higher accuracy (Hawkins et al., 1990), faster reaction times (Posner, 1980), and higher sensitivity (Sagi and Julesz, 1986) providing humans and non-human primates with a mechanism to select and prioritize spatial visual information (Carrasco, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spatial attention allows observers to detect targets with faster reaction times.
source: Deploying goal-directed spatial attention towards visual locations allows observers to detect targets with higher accuracy (Hawkins et al., 1990), faster reaction times (Posner, 1980), and higher sensitivity (Sagi and Julesz, 1986) providing humans and non-human primates with a mechanism to select and prioritize spatial visual information (Carrasco, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spatial attention allows observers to detect targets with higher sensitivity.
source: Deploying goal-directed spatial attention towards visual locations allows observers to detect targets with higher accuracy (Hawkins et al., 1990), faster reaction times (Posner, 1980), and higher sensitivity (Sagi and Julesz, 1986) providing humans and non-human primates with a mechanism to select and prioritize spatial visual information (Carrasco, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Enhanced behavioral responses during attention are accompanied by an increase in the gain of sensory responses near attended locations.
source: These enhanced behavioral responses are accompanied by both an increase in the gain of sensory responses near attended locations (Connor et al., 1996; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999) and changes in the shape and size of receptive fields, typically shrinking and shifting towards the target of attention (Ben Hamed et al., 2002; Womelsdorf et al., 2006; Anton-Erxleben et al., 2009; Klein et al., 2014; Kay et al., 2015; Vo et al., 2017; van Es et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: Enhanced behavioral responses during attention are accompanied by changes in the shape and size of receptive fields, typically shrinking and shifting towards the target of attention.
source: These enhanced behavioral responses are accompanied by both an increase in the gain of sensory responses near attended locations (Connor et al., 1996; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999) and changes in the shape and size of receptive fields, typically shrinking and shifting towards the target of attention (Ben Hamed et al., 2002; Womelsdorf et al., 2006; Anton-Erxleben et al., 2009; Klein et al., 2014; Kay et al., 2015; Vo et al., 2017; van Es et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: Shrinkage and shift of receptive fields toward attended targets has been observed in both single unit and population activity.
source: Shrinkage and shift of receptive fields toward attended targets has been observed in both single unit (Womelsdorf et al., 2006; Anton-Erxleben et al., 2009) and population (Klein et al., 2014; Vo et al., 2017; Fischer and Whitney, 2009; van Es et al., 2018) activity, and has been suggested to lead to behavioral enhancement through a variety of possible mechanisms (Anton-Erxleben and Carrasco, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: Receptive field changes might magnify the cortical representation of attended regions.
source: For example, receptive field changes might magnify the cortical representation of attended regions (Moran and Desimone, 1985), select for relevant information (Anton-Erxleben et al., 2009; Sprague and Serences, 2013), reduce uncertainty about spatial position (Vo et al., 2017), increase spatial discriminability (Kay et al., 2015; Fischer and Whitney, 2009), or change estimates of perceptual size (Anton-Erxleben et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical proposals.

claim: Shrinkage and shift of receptive fields has been hypothesized to occur as a side effect of increasing gain of neural responses.
source: Shrinkage and shift of receptive fields has also been hypothesized to occur as a side effect of increasing gain of neural responses (Klein et al., 2014; Compte and Wang, 2006), thus raising the question of which of these physiological effects could be responsible for enhanced perception.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: When gain is asymmetric across a receptive field, the overall effect will be to shift the receptive field location towards the side with the largest gain.
source: When gain is asymmetric across a receptive field, the overall effect will be to shift the receptive field location towards the side with the largest gain.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how asymmetric gain affects receptive field properties.

claim: Asymmetric gain can be expected to change spatial tuning properties such as the size and structure of the receptive field.
source: Similarly, asymmetric gain can be expected to change spatial tuning properties such as the size and structure of the receptive field.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how asymmetric gain affects receptive field properties.

claim: Increasing gain by itself has been hypothesized to be a mechanism for improving perceptual performance because response gain can increase the signal-to-noise ratio.
source: Increasing gain by itself has also been hypothesized to be a mechanism for improving perceptual performance, because response gain can increase the signal-to-noise ratio and make responses to different stimuli more discriminable (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Cohen and Newsome, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical proposals.

claim: Larger responses for attended stimuli can act to select relevant information when read-out through winner-take-all mechanisms.
source: Moreover, larger responses for attended stimuli can act to select relevant information when read-out through winner-take-all mechanisms (Lee et al., 1999; Pelli, 1985; Pestilli et al., 2011; Palmer et al., 2000; Hara et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical proposals.

claim: CNN architectures can be designed to closely mimic the primate visual hierarchy.
source: CNN architectures can be designed to closely mimic the primate visual hierarchy (Yamins et al., 2014; Kubilius et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Training units in CNNs to categorize images leads to visual filters that show a striking qualitative resemblance to the filters observed in early visual cortex.
source: Training 'units' in these networks to categorize images leads to visual filters that show a striking qualitative resemblance to the filters observed in early visual cortex (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) and the pattern of activity of these units when presented with natural images is sufficient to capture a large portion of the variance in neural activity in the retina (McIntosh et al., 2016), in early visual cortex (Cadena et al., 2019), and in later areas (Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015; Cichy et al., 2016; Eickenberg et al., 2017; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The pattern of activity of CNN units when presented with natural images is sufficient to capture a large portion of the variance in neural activity in the retina.
source: Training 'units' in these networks to categorize images leads to visual filters that show a striking qualitative resemblance to the filters observed in early visual cortex (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) and the pattern of activity of these units when presented with natural images is sufficient to capture a large portion of the variance in neural activity in the retina (McIntosh et al., 2016), in early visual cortex (Cadena et al., 2019), and in later areas (Güçlü and van Gerven, 2015; Cichy et al., 2016; Eickenberg et al., 2017; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014; Yamins et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cortical responses and neural network activity share a correlation structure across natural image categories.
source: Cortical responses and neural network activity also share a correlation structure across natural image categories (Storrs et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Gain changes introduced at the earliest stage in visual processing improved task performance with a magnitude comparable to that measured in human subjects.
source: Using simulations based on a CNN observer model we found that gain changes introduced at the earliest stage in visual processing improved task performance with a magnitude comparable to that measured in human subjects.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Gain changes induced changes in receptive field location, size, and spatial structure similar to that reported in physiological measurements.
source: While these gain changes also induced changes in receptive field location, size, and spatial structure similar to that reported in physiological measurements, these changes were neither necessary nor sufficient for improving model task performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results shown in Figure 3 and comparison to physiological literature.

claim: Changes in receptive field location, size, and spatial structure were neither necessary nor sufficient for improving model task performance.
source: While these gain changes also induced changes in receptive field location, size, and spatial structure similar to that reported in physiological measurements, these changes were neither necessary nor sufficient for improving model task performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results shown in Figures 4-7.

claim: Human observers improved their performance on the detection task when given a focal cue indicating the potential location of a target.
source: Human observers improved their performance on this detection task when given a focal cue indicating the potential location of a target (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: On distributed trials observers exceeded threshold performance (d'=1) at a stimulus duration of 155ms, 95% CI [135, 197].
source: On distributed trials observers exceeded threshold performance (d′=1) at a stimulus duration of 155ms, 95% CI [135, 197].
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: For focal trials, threshold performance (d'=1) was reached with only a 38ms [32, 43] stimulus duration.
source: For focal trials, the same threshold was reached with only a 38ms [32, 43] stimulus duration, demonstrating a substantial performance benefit of the focal cue.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: d' in the focal condition was higher than in the distributed condition, average increase across observers α=1.67× [1.57, 1.74].
source: We found that d′ in the focal condition was higher than in the distributed condition, average increase across observers α=1.67× [1.57, 1.74].
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The majority of the performance benefit from focal cues came from improved perceptual sensitivity, rather than speed-accuracy trade off.
source: Using a drift diffusion model, we found that the majority of this performance benefit came from improved perceptual sensitivity, rather than speed-accuracy trade off.
evidence: This claim is supported by drift diffusion model analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The average drift rate across observers in the focal condition was 1.61×, 95% CI [1.39, 1.77] the drift rate in the distributed condition.
source: Comparing the drift rate parameter we observed a similar effect to what was described above for d′: the average drift rate across observers in the focal condition was 1.61×, 95% CI [1.39, 1.77] the drift rate in the distributed condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by drift diffusion model analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: CORnet-Z is a four-layer CNN with repeated convolutional, rectified linear units (ReLU), and pooling.
source: CORnet-Z is a four-layer CNN with repeated convolutional, rectified linear units (ReLU), and pooling (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture used in the study.

claim: The trained prediction layers achieved a median AUC of 0.90, range [0.77, 0.96] on a held out validation set of 100 images.
source: On a separate held out validation set of 100 images, the trained prediction layers achieved a median AUC of 0.90, range [0.77, 0.96].
evidence: This claim is supported by evaluation of the trained classifiers.

claim: The model with 4× Gaussian gain had a median AUC across categories of 0.80, 95% CI [0.77, 0.82] compared to 0.71 [0.67, 0.72] without gain.
source: The model with this level of gain had a median AUC across categories of 0.80, 95% CI [0.77, 0.82] compared to 0.71 [0.67, 0.72] without gain and a median AUC improvement of 0.09 [0.08, 0.12] within each category.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model performance data.

claim: The gain strengths necessary to induce an increase in task performance in the neural network observer model were relatively large compared to the gain due to directed attention observed in measurements of single unit and population activity.
source: The gain strengths necessary to induce an increase in task performance in the neural network observer model were relatively large compared to the gain due to directed attention observed in measurements of single unit (Luck et al., 1997; Treue and Martínez Trujillo, 1999) and population (Birman and Gardner, 2019) activity.
evidence: This claim compares the model results to physiological measurements cited in the literature.

claim: A relatively small gain of 1.1× combined with an exponent of 3.8 led to a significantly larger effective gain of 1.37× after just one layer.
source: Using this approach, we found that a relatively small gain of 1.1× combined with an exponent of 3.8 led to a significantly larger effective gain of 1.37× after just one layer (Figure 3j).
evidence: This claim is supported by the nonlinear normalization analysis shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Static output non-linearities in single units range from about 2–4.
source: This form of non-linearity is consistent with the finding that static output non-linearities in single units range from about 2–4 (Gardner et al., 1999; Albrecht and Hamilton, 1982; Sclar et al., 1990; Heeger, 1992) and suggests a plausible physiological mechanism by which the larger gains predicted by our model could be implemented.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: The Gaussian gain applied to Layer 1 units caused the measured receptive field of units in Layer 4 to shift toward the locus of attention.
source: The Gaussian gain applied to Layer 1 units caused the measured receptive field (RF) of units in Layer 4 to shift (black ellipse, original; brown ellipse, with gain) toward the locus of attention (black ×).
evidence: This claim is supported by the receptive field analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The gain caused receptive fields to shift and shrink toward the locus of attention.
source: We found that the gain caused receptive fields to shift and shrink toward the locus of attention (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the receptive field analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The information provided by individual units in the model changed, increasing for units on the border of the cued quadrant.
source: The information provided by individual units in the model also changed, increasing for units on the border of the cued quadrant (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the information content analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The receptive field shift and shrinkage were magnified in deeper layers of the model.
source: The receptive field shift and shrinkage were magnified in deeper layers of the model (Figure 3d and e) consistent with physiological observations (Klein et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the layer-by-layer analysis shown in Figure 3d and e and comparison to physiological literature.

claim: The gain in activation strength propagated through the network without modification.
source: The gain in activation strength propagated through the network without modification (Figure 3f).
evidence: This claim is supported by the effective gain analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The model with receptive field shifts but no gain had no effect on task performance.
source: We found that the model with receptive field shifts but no gain had no effect on task performance, demonstrating that receptive field shifts are not key for the improvement in task performance observed with Gaussian gain (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by the shift-only model results shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The model imitating shifts from 4× Gaussian gain had a median AUC across categories of 0.71, 95% CI [0.66, 0.73] compared to 0.71 [0.67, 0.72] in the baseline model.
source: The model imitating shifts from 4× Gaussian gain had a median AUC across categories of 0.71, 95% CI [0.66, 0.73] compared to 0.71 [0.67, 0.72] in the baseline model, median change in AUC of –0.01 [-0.02, 0.01] within each category.
evidence: This claim is supported by the shift-only model performance data.

claim: The receptive field structure model was unable to account for the behavioral effects of the Gaussian gain.
source: The receptive field structure model, like the shift model, was unable to account for the behavioral effects of the Gaussian gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by the receptive field structure model results shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The shrinkage model was unable to account for improved task performance with Gaussian gain.
source: The shrinkage model was unable to account for improved task performance with Gaussian gain.
evidence: This claim is supported by the shrinkage model results shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Using the gain-only model we were able to reproduce the improved task performance of the original Gaussian gain.
source: Using the gain-only model we were able to reproduce the improved task performance of the original Gaussian gain (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gain-only model results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The median AUC across categories of the 4× flat gain model was 0.78, 95% CI [0.76, 0.83] compared to 0.80 [0.77, 0.82] for the 4× Gaussian gain model.
source: The median AUC across categories of the 4× flat gain model was 0.78, 95% CI [0.76, 0.83] compared to 0.80 [0.77, 0.82] for the 4× Gaussian gain model.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gain-only model performance data.

claim: The propagated gain map, when used to multiply the outputs of a model with no Gaussian gain, was sufficient to induce task performance benefits similar to Gaussian gain applied to the input.
source: We found that the propagated gain map, when used to multiply the outputs of a model with no Gaussian gain (Multiply by propagated gain, Figure 8a) was sufficient to induce task performance benefits similar to Gaussian gain applied to the input (Propagated gain vs. Gaussian gain, Figure 8c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sufficiency test results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The behavioral effect of an early gain was mostly reversed by dividing the final layer activations by the propagated gain map.
source: To test the hypothesis that gain was necessary to account for the behavioral effect, we divided the final layer activations by the propagated gain map (Divide by propagated gain, Figure 8a). We found that the behavioral effect of an early gain was mostly reversed by this manipulation (Removed gain vs. Distributed, Figure 8c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the necessity test results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Spatial gain implemented by neural populations in visual cortex can be sufficient to induce behavioral effects of attention for both detection and discrimination even without the concomitant changes in downstream receptive field properties.
source: Our results suggest that spatial gain implemented by neural populations in visual cortex can be sufficient to induce behavioral effects of attention for both detection and discrimination even without the concomitant changes in downstream receptive field properties.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results from the various model manipulations.

claim: Increasing response magnitudes through gain changes can act to select relevant visual information when coupled with a max or soft-max pooling to suppress irrelevant visual information which has a lower response magnitude.
source: That is, increasing response magnitudes through gain changes can act to select relevant visual information when coupled with a max or soft-max pooling to suppress irrelevant visual information which has a lower response magnitude (Lee et al., 1999; Pestilli et al., 2011; Hara et al., 2014; Pelli, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical proposals and the model results.

claim: Changes in receptive field properties may be secondary effects and only a consequence of applying gain, rather than the cause of the behavioral improvements.
source: Although increasing gain can have downstream effects on receptive field properties such as changes in position, size and spatial structure, our results suggest that these may be secondary effects and only a consequence of applying gain, rather than the cause of the behavioral improvements as others have suggested (Anton-Erxleben and Carrasco, 2013; Moran and Desimone, 1985; Anton-Erxleben et al., 2009; Sprague and Serences, 2013; Vo et al., 2017; Kay et al., 2015; Fischer and Whitney, 2009; Anton-Erxleben et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and contrasts with prior theoretical proposals.

claim: Gain had no additional impact when the readout was already spatially specific.
source: In addition, we found that gain had no additional impact when the readout was already spatially specific, reinforcing the interpretation that gain and selection of relevant information are intertwined.
evidence: This claim is supported by the 4×4 readout analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model architecture allowed examination of how gain at the earliest stages of processing causes changes in spatial receptive field properties.
source: In our case, the advantage of this approach is that the model architecture allowed us to examine how gain at the earliest stages of processing causes changes in spatial receptive field properties: any time a gain occurs in an asymmetrical manner across a receptive field, downstream units will experience an apparent shift as well as shrinkage or expansion.
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling approach and its advantages.

claim: If changes in spatial receptive field properties are the consequence of gain changes, then it raises the question of whether these receptive field changes actually help to improve task performance.
source: However, if changes in spatial receptive field properties are the consequence of gain changes (Klein et al., 2014; Compte and Wang, 2006), then it raises the question of whether these receptive field changes actually help to improve task performance.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the hypothesis that receptive field changes are consequences of gain.

claim: Previous modeling work has demonstrated that shift and shrinkage can increase the resolution and redundancy of receptive field coverage.
source: Nevertheless, previous modeling work has demonstrated that shift and shrinkage, in particular, can increase the resolution and redundancy of receptive field coverage (Kay et al., 2015; Vo et al., 2017; Theiss et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling studies.

claim: The results differ from previous modeling work along two important dimensions: the magnitude of shift, shrinkage, and sensitivity changes were scaled to those induced by Gaussian gain matched to human performance, and the results were based only on simulations for category detection and discrimination tasks.
source: Our results differ along two important dimensions: first, we scaled the magnitude of shift, shrinkage, and sensitivity changes to those induced by Gaussian gain (at a gain strength that was matched to human performance) and these were in general equal to or smaller in magnitude to what was observed in these previous papers. This leaves open the possibility that larger shifts or shrinkage could have a more direct impact on task performance. We also note that our results were based only on simulations for category detection and discrimination tasks.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study to prior work, explaining differences in approach and scope.

claim: Other tasks which depend more directly on spatial coding, such as judgements of visual position, could exhibit larger benefits from shifts and shrinkage of receptive fields.
source: It may be the case that other tasks which depend more directly on spatial coding, such as judgements of visual position, could exhibit larger benefits from shifts and shrinkage of receptive fields (Kay et al., 2015; Vo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation about how the results might differ for other types of tasks.

claim: CORnet was designed to reflect the primate visual system and has been evaluated by comparing the similarity of CNN unit activity against measurements of single unit activity in the primate visual cortex.
source: We chose to analyze a CNN whose architecture was designed to reflect the primate visual system. This has been evaluated by comparing the similarity of CNN unit activity against measurements of single unit activity in the primate visual cortex (Schrimpf et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior validation work.

claim: After training, the image features that the CNN units become selective for align closely with those that activate single units in visual cortex.
source: After training, the image features that the CNN units become selective for align closely with those that activate single units in visual cortex (Yamins et al., 2014; Carter et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CORnet differs from the visual system in that it is a completely feed-forward model.
source: While CORnet was designed to map individual visual cortex regions onto the different layers of the CNN, it differs from the visual system in that it is a completely feed-forward model.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the model architecture.

claim: The visual system has recurrence both within and between visual areas.
source: It is well-known that the visual system has recurrence both within and between visual areas (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Computational modeling has suggested that recurrence can affect how gain and additive offsets change down stream receptive field location and size, in particular enhancing these effects beyond receptive field boundaries.
source: Computational modeling has suggested that recurrence can affect how gain and additive offsets change down stream receptive field location and size, in particular enhancing these effects beyond receptive field boundaries (Compte and Wang, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior modeling work.

claim: More realistic models could have even stronger downstream effects on spatial receptive field properties than what was documented in a purely feed-forward network.
source: These considerations suggest that more realistic models could have even stronger downstream effects on spatial receptive field properties then what we have documented in a purely feed-forward network.
evidence: This is a speculation about how results might differ in more realistic models.

claim: CORnet is missing many intermediate areas of the visual system (notably area V3).
source: CORnet is also missing many intermediate areas of the visual system (notably area V3) (Wandell and Winawer, 2011) as well as an explicit gain control mechanism such as divisive normalization (Carandini and Heeger, 2012) which might account for the large gain necessary in our model to produce human-like performance enhancements.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of the model architecture.

claim: The 4× gain should be interpreted as both an explicit increase in gain as well as an implicit gain due to the effects of normalization.
source: Instead, in our model, the 4× gain should be interpreted as both an explicit increase in gain as well as an implicit gain due to the effects of normalization (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Carandini and Heeger, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results in the context of normalization mechanisms.

claim: A physiologically plausible gain of 1.1×, when accentuated by a divisive gain control mechanism and amplified across multiple visual areas, could have produced the magnitude of effects necessary for human-level improvements in task performance.
source: We assessed how these effects might interact in our CNN by demonstrating that a physiologically plausible gain of 1.1×, when accentuated by a divisive gain control mechanism (Kaiser et al., 2016; Carandini and Heeger, 2012) and amplified across multiple visual areas (many of which are not included in the CORnet model), could have produced the magnitude of effects necessary for human-level improvements in task performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the nonlinear normalization analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: Gain changes on the order 20–40% (1.2–1.4×) have been measured in neural recordings in primates.
source: This smaller gain is more consistent with neural recordings in primates, where gain changes on the order 20–40% (1.2–1.4×) have been measured (Motter, 1993; Luck et al., 1997; Treue and Martínez Trujillo, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: Physiological measurements have found evidence for early gain.
source: Physiological measurements have found evidence for early gain (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Motter, 1993; Luck et al., 1997), but it is equally possible that the gain is applied at a late stage close to decision making and signal gains early in visual cortex are a result of backward projections to these areas (Buffalo et al., 2010; Moore and Armstrong, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claim: The propagated gain analysis confirms that gain signals with spatial specificity arriving at later stages in processing would have similar effects on task performance.
source: The propagated gain analysis confirms that gain signals with spatial specificity arriving at later stages in processing (Moore and Armstrong, 2003) would have similar effects on task performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the propagated gain analysis results.

claim: In biological systems, the mechanisms of attention are intertwined: changes to early sensory signals will have complex effects on the later stages that are used for readout.
source: In biological systems, these mechanisms are intertwined: as we have shown, changes to early sensory signals will have complex effects on the later stages that are used for readout.
evidence: This is a general statement about biological systems supported by the modeling results.

claim: In an idealized model, the changes that would have the most effect on the readout would be computed by approximating their gradients on the decision axis.
source: In an idealized model, the changes that would have the most effect on the readout would be computed by approximating their gradients on the decision axis (Lindsay and Miller, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: It is not known whether or how gradients similar to those computed through back-propagation can be computed in biological systems.
source: However, these gradients are typically computed in models through back-propagation (Rumelhart et al., 1986), and it is not known whether or how similar gradients can be computed in biological systems.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation in understanding biological computation.

claim: In the limit, shift, shrinkage, and tuning changes in receptive fields must have an impact on sensory representations and therefore on performance.
source: In the limit, shift, shrinkage, and tuning changes in receptive fields must have an impact on sensory representations and therefore on performance.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the theoretical limits of receptive field changes.

claim: At the scale expected in the primate visual system during goal-directed behavior, receptive field changes are not sufficient to produce the expected effects of spatial attention on task performance.
source: But our results show that in a neural network model and at the scale expected in the primate visual system during goal-directed behavior, these are not sufficient to produce the expected effects of spatial attention on task performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Gain combined with a nonlinear selection mechanism meets the demands imposed by goal-directed visual attention.
source: Instead, gain combined with a nonlinear selection mechanism meets the demands imposed by goal-directed visual attention.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: The main prediction of the model is that spatial visual attention relies primarily on changes in gain and not concomitant downstream effects to spatial receptive field properties.
source: Such interventions would allow for testing the main prediction of our model: that spatial visual attention relies primarily on changes in gain and not concomitant downstream effects to spatial receptive field properties.
evidence: This is a statement of the main prediction of the model.

claim: Seven observers participated in the experiments (1 female, 6 male, mean age 22 y, range 19–24).
source: Seven observers were observers for the experiments (1 female, 6 male, mean age 22 y, range 19–24).
evidence: This is a description of the participant demographics.

claim: Procedures were approved in advance by the Stanford Institutional Review Board on human participants research.
source: Procedures were approved in advance by the Stanford Institutional Review Board on human participants research and all observers gave prior written informed consent before participating (Protocol IRB-32120).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: Visual stimuli were generated using MATLAB and MGL.
source: Visual stimuli were generated using MATLAB (The Mathworks, Inc) and MGL (Gardner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Stimuli were displayed at 60 cm viewing distance on a 22.5 inch VIEWPixx LCD display.
source: Stimuli were displayed at 60 cm viewing distance on a 22.5 inch VIEWPixx LCD display (resolution of 1900x1200, refresh-rate of 120 Hz) and responses collected via keyboard.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: Eye-tracking was performed using an infrared video-based eye-tracker at 500 Hz.
source: Eye-tracking was performed using an infrared video-based eye-tracker at 500 Hz (Eyelink 1000; SR Research).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The stimuli presented to both humans and the neural network observer model were composed of four base images arranged in a grid.
source: In the object detection task, the stimuli presented to both humans and the neural network observer model were composed of four base images arranged in a grid (henceforth a 'composite grid').
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus design.

claim: 929 images were pulled from each of 21 ImageNet categories.
source: We pulled 929 images from each of 21 ImageNet categories: analog clock (renamed to 'clock'), artichoke, bakery (renamed to 'baked goods'), banana, bathtub, bonsai tree (renamed to 'tree'), cabbage butterfly, coffee, computer, Ferris wheel, football helmet, garden spider (renamed to 'spider'), greenhouse, home theater, long-horned beetle (renamed to 'beetle'), mortar, padlock, paintbrush, seashore, stone wall, and toaster.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus set.

claim: CORnet-Z is a convolutional neural network proposed by Kubilius et al., 2018.
source: We modeled the ventral visual pathway using CORnet-Z, a convolutional neural network (CNN) proposed by Kubilius et al., 2018.
evidence: This is a description of the model used in the study.

claim: The model consists of four convolutional layers producing feature maps of decreasing spatial resolution.
source: The model consists of four convolutional layers producing feature maps of decreasing spatial resolution (Table 2).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: The model which was used was pre-trained on ImageNet by the original authors.
source: The model which we used was pre-trained on ImageNet by the original authors (Kubilius et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the model training.

claim: To allow the neural network observer model to perform an object detection task, a set of linear classifiers was trained on the model output to predict the presence or absence of each of the twenty target categories.
source: To allow the neural network observer model to perform an object detection task, we trained a set of linear classifiers on the model output to predict the presence or absence of each of the twenty target categories.
evidence: This is a description of the model training procedure.

claim: Weights were fit using logistic regression with L2 regularization, using scikit-learn and the LIBLINEAR package.
source: Weights were fit using logistic regression with L2 regularization, using scikit-learn and the LIBLINEAR package (Pedregosa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the model training procedure.

claim: The Gaussian was centered in the cued quadrant and σ was set to 56 pixels (approx 2.5 degrees).
source: The Gaussian was centered in the cued quadrant and σ was set to 56 pixels (approx 2.5 degrees).
evidence: This is a description of the Gaussian gain parameters.

claim: Four values of β were explored: 1.1, 2, 4, and 11.
source: We explored four values of β: 1.1, 2, 4, and 11.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: 300 units per layer (1200 total units) were randomly sampled for receptive field analysis.
source: To reduce computational requirements we randomly sampled 300 units per layer (1200 total units) for receptive field analysis, with higher density near the attended locus.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis methods.

claim: To determine the location and size of the receptive field of each CNN unit, the derivative of their activation with respect to the pixels in the input image was computed.
source: To determine the location and size of the receptive field of each CNN unit, we computed the derivative of their activation with respect to the pixels in the input image.
evidence: This is a description of the receptive field measurement method.

claim: Effective gain was defined as the ratio between the standard deviation of a unit's activity after applying an attention mechanism compared to before.
source: We defined effective gain as the ratio between the standard deviation of a unit's activity after applying an attention mechanism compared to before.
evidence: This is a description of the effective gain measurement.
